Modular assembly of complex C-alkyl glycoside enabled via
cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis
Rui-Qiang Jiao<sup>1</sup>, Ming Li<sup>2</sup>, Xi Chen<sup>1</sup>, Mei-Ze Xu<sup>1</sup>, Tian Ding<sup>1</sup>, Xiao-Ping Gong<sup>1</sup>, Zhuo-Mei Li<sup>1</sup>,
Xue-Yuan Liu<sup>1*</sup> & Yong-Min Liang<sup>1</sup>
<sup>1</sup>State Key Laboratory of Applied Organic Chemistry, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou 730000, China
<sup>2</sup>College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou 730070, China
Received July 31, 2024; accepted October 8, 2024; published online January 2, 2025
C-Alkyl glycosides are found in natural products and are indispensable in drug development programs, owing to their diverse
range of medicinal properties. Two-component reactions involving glycosyl radical addition are well documented and proved
efficient for the C-alkyl glycosides synthesis. However, multicomponent reactions for the rapid and controllable construction of
structurally diversified C-alkyl glycosides in a single step remains a significant challenge due to the issues associated with
balancing reactivity, compatibility, and selectivity. Herein, we report an NHC and photoredox co-catalyzed three-component
method to access complex and valuable C-alkyl glycosides. This protocol exhibits broad substrate scope and excellent chemo-
and regioselectivity. Furthermore, nine types of sugars are compatible with this reaction. In addition, the generality of this
catalytic strategy was further highlighted by the potential for scalable production, the feasibility of further modifications of the
products and its successful application in the late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutical skeletons.
C-alkyl glycosides, three-component, NHC catalysis, visible-light photoredox catalysis, radical-radical coupling

1 Introduction
C-Alkylglycosides are an important class of carbohydrate
scaffolds that are prevalent structural motifs in biologically
relevant molecules as key structural elements (Scheme 1a)
[1]. Compared with O-glycosides, their stability in vitro and
in vivo is obviously enhanced, which plays an important role
in the modern design of C-glycoside drug candidates and
studies of important biological processes [2].
Considering the important biological activity and medical
value of C-alkylglycosides, as such, the development of
synthetic methods for C-alkylglycosides is an unmet need for
organic chemists. The generation of glycosyl radical inter-
mediates provides an efficient strategy for the synthesis ofC-
glycosides [3–10]. Among those approaches, the addition of
glycosyl radicals across alkenes has evolved to a key strategy
for the synthesis of C-alkylglycosides (Scheme 1b) [3,7–10].
Inspired by Giese’s pioneering work [9a] on the use of tri-
butyltin hydride under photolysis conditions, so far, many
research groups have explored the Sn- [9a,9e], Et B-
[9m,9n], AIBN- [9h], or Sm-mediated [7a,7c,7d] and Ni-
[9f], Ru- [9j,9i], Fe- [9o], or Ti-catalyzed [9l] Giese reactions
for C-alkylglycosides. These reactions, which can be con-
ducted under practical and mild conditions, feature high
functional group tolerance and broad substrate scope. Re-
cently, Hu’s group [11] realized the synthesis of gem-di-
fluoroalkene-containing C-alkylglycosides via
a
photomediated defluorinative gem-difluoroallylation reac-
tion. Very recently, our group reported the synthesis C-alkyl
glycosides of α-aryl-β-glycosamide via Smiles rearrange-
ment [12]. Despite the significant progress recorded in this
field, the intermolecular three-component cascade reactions
for molecular complexity C-alkylglycosides synthesis has
been far less developed. There is only one example, in 2023,
Ackermann’s group [13] achieved a domino meta-C–H
ethylglycosylation by merging the addition of glycosyl ra-
dicals to olefins and ruthenium catalysis for distal C–H ac-
tivation three-component radical cross-coupling reactions.
As a result, the development of a new method involving the
glycosyl radical intermolecular three-component cascade
reactions for complex molecules C-alkylglycosides synthesis
is greatly desired.

reactions for complex molecules C-alkylglycosides synthesis
is greatly desired.
In recent years, the combination of visible light and NHC
cocatalyzed radical coupling reactions has generated recent
excitement to drive complex bond constructions. The key
step ofthe reaction is radical and ketyl radical cross-coupling
delivers a ketone-containing product. So far, many elegant
works have been well-established by Ohmiya and other
groups [14]. On the other hand, 1,4-difunctionalization of
1,3-enynes via a radical pathway has also been intensively
investigated recently [15]. However, NHC-promoted radical
1,4-difunctionalization of1,3-enynes remains a challenge for
the synthesis of functionalized allenes ketones. Du [16],
Huang [17], Hong [18] and Zhang et al. [19] independently
developed a NHC-promoted radical 1,4-difunctionalization
of 1,3-enynes, providing a ready access to different sub-
stituted allenyl ketones. Despite significant progress, it is
surprising to observe that NHC-promoted radical 1,4-gly-
cosylacylation of 1,3-enynes has not yet been explored.
Considering the importance of the complex molecules C-
alkylglycosides in medicinal chemistry and inspired by
previous work, we wondered whether the combination of
glycosyl radical addition and NHC and photoredox catalysis
could be feasible for modular assembly of complex C-al-
kylglycosides. With our group’s ongoing research on C-
glycosylation, herein, we report an NHC and photoredox co-
catalyzed three-component reaction from readily available
1,3-enynes, aroyl fluorides, glycosyl bromides. This trans-
formation involves the coupling of ketyl radical from single
electron transfer (SET) reduction of in situ formed acyla-
zolium ions and allenyl radical from glycosyl radicals se-
lectively attacks the olefin unit of the 1,3-enyne to produce
the propargyl radical intermediate, which could undergo
reversible resonance, providing direct access to an array of
complex and structurally diversified valuable C-alkyl gly-
cosides under mild, transition-metal-free conditions.
2 Experimental
In a 10 mL pre-dried schlenk tube with stir bar, (TMS) SiOH
(39 mg, 0.15 mmol, 1.5 equiv.), glycosylbromide 2a
(0.25 mmol, 2.5 equiv.), PC1 (4.2 mg, 3 mol%), NHC-A
(8.3 mg, 20 mol%), and K CO (41.4 mg, 0.3 mmol, 3.0
equiv.) were added. The tube was charged with argon, which
repeated more than three times. Subsequently, 1 mL MeCN
was injected and 1a (0.1 mmol) and 3a (0.2 mmol) were
added. Then the reaction mixture was irradiated with blue
light-emitting diode (LED) at room temperature for 12 h.
After the reaction completed, the solvent was evaporated
under vacuum. The residue was purified by flash chroma-
tography on silica gel (petroleum ether/ethyl acetate = 3:1) to
afford the corresponding product 4a.

We subsequently investigated the generality of 1,3-enynes.
As shown in Table 3, 1,3-enynes bearing electron-donating
(–OMe, –Me) or -withdrawing substituents (–F, Cl, Br) at the
para-positions of the 2-phenyl rings (5a–5e) exhibited good
reactivity and promoted reactions smoothly in good yields
(56%–68%). The substituents at the ortho-position or meta-
position also worked well to provide the target product (5f–
5i) in moderate to good yields (53%–67%). Furthermore,
substrates with 1-naphthalene and heterocycles were also
amenable to this catalytic process and afforded the desired
products (5j, 5k) in comparable yields. Besides, 2-alkyl
substituted 1,3-enynes were applicable, giving the desired
products (5l).
We also explored the scope of acyl fluorides. As shown in
Table 4, The electron-donating groups at the aromatic ring’s
para-, meta-, or ortho-position reacted efficiently to furnish
the corresponding products under these reaction conditions
in 65%–72% yields (6a, 6b, 6e, 6g), while the electron-
withdrawing groups at the aromatic ring’s para- or ortho-
position led to low efficiency (6c, 6d, 6f). Furthermore,
multi-substituted aryl acyl fluorides were also tolerated and
delivered the expected products 6h in yields of 62%. Sub-
strates with 2-naphthalene moieties could also give the de-
sired products in 51% yield 6i. Additionally, to our surprise,
heterocycles like thiophene, furan and pyridine, which have
frequently been found in medicinal chemistry due to their
various biological activities, were found to be compatible
with the reaction conditions (6j–6l).

4 Conclusions
In summary, we have developed a strategy to accomplish
multicomponent assembly of complex C-alkyl glycoside via

cooperative NHC and photoredox catalysis under mild,
transition-metal-free conditions. This multicomponent cou-
pling reaction used readily available starting materials with
broad functional group compatibility and excellent chemo-
and regionselectivity. Mechanistic studies suggest that this
transformation proceeds via radical/radical cross coupling of
ketyl radicals with allenyl radicals. The ketyl radicals are
generated via SET reduction of in situ formed acylazolium
ions whereas the allenyl radicals derive from chemo-specific
glycosyl radical addition to the 1,3-enynes. We expect that
this protocol will provide a versatile platform for the multi-
component assembly of complex C-alkyl glycosides and
believe this work will stimulate more research in multi-
component reactions for the preparation of structurally di-
versified valuable C-alkyl glycosides that are difficult-to-
made in future.
